sections.normalized_html:
A walk of length [MATH: n] in an undirected graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where the edge [MATH: e_i] is incident on vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_{i+1}] for each [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows: [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} \cdots \overset{e_n}{-} v_{n+1}] Suppose the graph has no multiple (parallel) edges. In that case, we can drop the [MATH: e_i]'s in the above notation since any corresponding pair of incident vertices will uniquely determine any edge.

A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.

A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, it's a walk since we can write it as [MATH: v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} v_4 \overset{e_9}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} v_4] where vertices and edges can be repeated.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, it's a trail since we can write it as [MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_9}{-} v_4 \overset{e_4}{-} v_5 \overset{e_5}{-} v_6 \overset{e_{11}}{-} v_8 \overset{e_8}{-} v_1] where all edges are distinct.

  • Statement III is false. Notice that it's not a walk, and consequently, it is not a path: no edge directly joins vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_3.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Content:
In a weighted graph, a numerical value (called a weight) is associated with each edge. Although weights can be any real numbers, only positive numbers are usually used for most practical purposes.

Content:
In visual representations, weights are shown as numbers or labels directly on the edges. For example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e53905e52c8bbb11549845c9906db5c2]

Content:
The weight of a walk (also referred to as length or cost) in a weighted graph is the sum of the weights of the traversed edges. The same definition applies to trails and paths. We denote the weight of a walk [MATH: w] as [MATH: |w|,] and also [MATH: \ell(w)] when referring to it as length.

Content:
For example, consider the walk [MATH: w_1] in the graph above.
[MATH: w_1=v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_2 - v_3 - v_2]

Content:
This walk consists of five edges, so its weight is equal to the sum of their weights:

Content:
[MATH: |w_1|=9+3+3+8+8=31]

Graphic:

Content:
The distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in a weighted graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the weight of the shortest path (the path with the least weight) from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v.] As in unweighted graphs, if no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, the distance is considered [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
For example, in the graph above, the shortest path from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_3] is [MATH: (v_1 - v_5 - v_4 - v_3);] therefore, the distance is
[MATH: d(v_1, v_3)=8+1+7=16]

If no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, we say that the distance is [MATH: \infty.]

In our case, the shortest path from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_5] is [MATH: v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_5] that contains [MATH: 3] edges of cumulative length of [MATH: 6+5+7=18.]

Therefore, [MATH: d(v_1,v_5)=18.]

Note: There are other paths from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_5] with equal or fewer number of edges. However, the cumulative length of these paths is greater than [MATH: 18.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A walk [MATH: w] of length [MATH: n] in an undirected graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where the edge [MATH: e_i] is incident on vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_{i+1}] for each [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows:
[MATH: w=v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} \cdots \overset{e_n}{-} v_{n+1}]

Content:
In a walk, it is possible to visit any vertex or traverse any edge multiple times. For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5f417ba8595aaad65c2da50d1c1c2ccc]

Content:
Notice that the walk [MATH: w_1] visits vertex [MATH: v_2] three times and traverses edges [MATH: e_2] and [MATH: e_5] twice each.

Content:
[MATH: w_1=v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_5}{-} v_4 \overset{e_5}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_2}{-} v_2]

Content:
In a graph with no parallel edges, we usually omit the [MATH: e_i]'s in the above notation since any corresponding pair of incident vertices uniquely determines an edge. Thus, the walk above can be written equally correctly as follows:

Content:
[MATH: w_1=v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_2 - v_3 - v_2]

Content:
A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct. The walk [MATH: w_1] above is not a trail because it includes the repeated edges [MATH: e_2] and [MATH: e_5.] As an example of a trail, consider the same graph, but with a new walk highlighted.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/92cef1b7639d3d7dee362820ba18ae67]

Content:
The walk [MATH: w_2] is a valid trail because, although it has the repeated vertex [MATH: v_2,] all its edges are distinct.

Content:
[MATH: w_2=v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_3 - v_2 - v_5]

Content:
A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct. Neither [MATH: w_1] nor [MATH: w_2] above is a path because they have the repeated vertex [MATH: v_2]. As an example of a path , consider the same graph, but with a new walk highlighted.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cd449fce0ac2e17922d3c2251fe551f1]

Content:
The walk [MATH: w_3] is a valid path because it does not contain any repeated vertices or edges.

Content:
[MATH: w_3=v_5 - v_2 - v_3 - v_4]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Walks, Trails, and Paths in Undirected Graphs

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/bfa03ff87fe442fcbc6c0138cc6a9224]

Which of the following statements are true about the graph shown above?

1. [MATH: v_2 - v_3 - v_4 - v_2 - v_3 - v_4] is a walk
2. [MATH: v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_5 - v_6 - v_8 - v_1] is a trail
3. [MATH: v_1 - v_3 - v_5 - v_7] is a path

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A walk of length [MATH: n] in an undirected graph is a sequence of [MATH: n] edges [MATH: e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_n] with the associated vertices [MATH: v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{n+1}] where the edge [MATH: e_i] is incident on vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_{i+1}] for each [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n.] This can be written as follows:
[MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} \cdots \overset{e_n}{-} v_{n+1}]
Suppose the graph has no multiple (parallel) edges. In that case, we can drop the [MATH: e_i]'s in the above notation since any corresponding pair of incident vertices will uniquely determine any edge.

A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.

A path is a walk in which all vertices (and, as a result, all edges) are distinct.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, it's a walk since we can write it as
[MATH: v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} v_4 \overset{e_9}{-} v_2 \overset{e_2}{-} v_3 \overset{e_3}{-} v_4]
where vertices and edges can be repeated.
- Statement II is true. Indeed, it's a trail since we can write it as
[MATH: v_1 \overset{e_1}{-} v_2 \overset{e_9}{-} v_4 \overset{e_4}{-} v_5 \overset{e_5}{-} v_6 \overset{e_{11}}{-} v_8 \overset{e_8}{-} v_1]
where all edges are distinct.
- Statement III is false. Notice that it's not a walk, and consequently, it is not a path: no edge directly joins vertices [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_3.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Item 5 — Tutorial: Distances

Content:
The distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in a graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the length (i.e., the number of edges) of the shortest path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v.] If no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, we say that the distance is [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8faed092f37a14206d21a4fe32c4c9c5]

Content:
Let's determine the distances between the following vertices:

Content:
- The shortest path from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_4] is [MATH: v_1-v_2-v_4.] It consists of [MATH: 2] edges. Thus,

Content:
[MATH: d(v_{1}, v_{4})|= 2]

Content:
- The shortest path from [MATH: v_5] to [MATH: v_8] is [MATH: v_5-v_6-v_7-v_8.] It consists of [MATH: 3] edges. Thus,

Content:
[MATH: d(v_{5}, v_{8})|= 3]

Content:
- There are no paths from [MATH: v_2] to [MATH: v_5.] Thus,

Content:
[MATH: d(v_{2}, v_{5})|= ∞]

Content:
Several algorithms exist to find the shortest path between two vertices in a graph; they will be discussed in future lessons.

Item 6 — Tutorial: Weighted Graphs

Content:
In a weighted graph, a numerical value (called a weight) is associated with each edge. Although weights can be any real numbers, only positive numbers are usually used for most practical purposes.

Content:
In visual representations, weights are shown as numbers or labels directly on the edges. For example:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e53905e52c8bbb11549845c9906db5c2]

Content:
The weight of a walk (also referred to as length or cost) in a weighted graph is the sum of the weights of the traversed edges. The same definition applies to trails and paths. We denote the weight of a walk [MATH: w] as [MATH: |w|,] and also [MATH: \ell(w)] when referring to it as length.

Content:
For example, consider the walk [MATH: w_1] in the graph above.
[MATH: w_1=v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_2 - v_3 - v_2]

Content:
This walk consists of five edges, so its weight is equal to the sum of their weights:

Content:
[MATH: |w_1|=9+3+3+8+8=31]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d3a9099f4fba349cd10149f1cd99465f]

Content:
The distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in a weighted graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the weight of the shortest path (the path with the least weight) from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v.] As in unweighted graphs, if no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, the distance is considered [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
For example, in the graph above, the shortest path from [MATH: v_1] to [MATH: v_3] is [MATH: (v_1 - v_5 - v_4 - v_3);] therefore, the distance is
[MATH: d(v_1, v_3)=8+1+7=16]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Defining Eccentricity, Radius, Diameter, and Center for Unweighted Graphs

Content:
The eccentricity of a vertex [MATH: v] in a graph [MATH: G=(V,E),] denoted [MATH: \epsilon(v),] is the maximum distance between [MATH: v] and any other vertex of the graph:
[MATH: \epsilon(v) = \max_{w \in V} \left\{ d(v,w) \right\}]
If there is at least one vertex [MATH: w] such that no path exists from [MATH: v] to [MATH: w,] then [MATH: \epsilon(v)] is considered [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G_1] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6e6e6ec866def9479825479d6cf27876]

Content:
In this graph, [MATH: d(v_1,v_7)=3] because the shortest path is [MATH: (v_1 - v_2 - v_4 - v_7).] By symmetry, [MATH: d(v_5,v_6)=3.]

Content:
From any of the three remaining vertices [MATH: v_2, v_3,] and [MATH: v_4,] any other vertex can be reached by traversing at most two edges.

Content:
Therefore, the eccentricities of the vertices are as follows:

Content:
| Vertex, [MATH: v] | [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: v_2] | [MATH: v_3] | [MATH: v_4] | [MATH: v_5] | [MATH: v_6] | [MATH: v_7] |
| Eccentricity, [MATH: \epsilon(v)] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 3] |

Content:
The following three graph parameters (namely, radius, diameter, and center) are based on the concept of eccentricity.

Content:
The radius of the graph is the minimum eccentricity of the graph's vertices:
[MATH: r(G) = \min_{v \in V} \{ \epsilon(v) \}]

Content:
In the graph above, the minimum eccentricity is [MATH: 2;] hence, [MATH: r(G_1)=2.]

Content:
The diameter of the graph is the maximum eccentricity of the graph vertices (alternatively, the diameter is the longest possible distance between the vertices of the graph):

Content:
[MATH: d(G) = \max_{v \in V} \{ \epsilon(v) \} = \max_{v, w \in V} \{ d(v,w) \}]

Content:
In the graph above, the maximum eccentricity is [MATH: 3;] hence, [MATH: d(G_1)=3.]

Content:
In geometry, the diameter of a circle is always twice the radius. This is not the case for radii and diameters in graphs, as illustrated by the example above, where [MATH: d=1.5r.] For connected graphs, the following inequality holds:
[MATH: \text{radius} \leq \textrm{diameter} \leq 2 \cdot \textrm{radius}]

Content:
You'll learn more about connected graphs in future lessons.

Content:
The center of a graph is the set of all vertices with the minimum eccentricity (i.e., the graph's radius).

Content:
[MATH: {v ∈ V: ϵ(v) = r(G)}]

Content:
In the graph above, three vertices have the minimum eccentricity of [MATH: 2;] hence, the center of [MATH: G_1] is [MATH: \{v_2, v_3, v_4\}.]

Item 11 — Example: Finding Numerical Characteristics of a Graph

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/31bff92ef6c09ea27c256744a15d6554]

Find the radius [MATH: r(G)] and the diameter [MATH: d(G)] of the graph [MATH: G] above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The eccentricity of a graph vertex [MATH: v] in a connected graph [MATH: G] is the maximum distance between [MATH: v] and other vertex of the graph:
[MATH: \epsilon(v) = \max_{w \in V} \{ d(v,w) \},]
where [MATH: V] is the set of graph vertices.

The radius of the graph is the minimum eccentricity of the graph vertices:
[MATH: r(G) = \min_{v \in V} \{ \epsilon(v) \}]

The diameter of the graph is the maximum eccentricity of the graph vertices (alternatively, the diameter is the longest possible distance between the vertices of the graph):

[MATH: d(G) = \max_{v \in V} \{ \epsilon(v) \} = \max_{v, w \in V} \{ d(v,w) \}]

In our case, the eccentricities of the vertices are as follows:

[MATH: ϵ(v_{1})|= 2; ϵ(v_{2})|= 3; ϵ(v_{3})|= 4; ϵ(v_{4})|= 4; ϵ(v_{5})|= 3; ϵ(v_{6})|= 4; ϵ(v_{7})|= 4]

Therefore, the required radius and diameter are
[MATH: r(G) = min_(v ∈ V){ϵ(v)} = 2,; d(G) = max_(v ∈ V){ϵ(v)} = 4.]

Note: For any connected graph, we have the following inequality:
[MATH: \text{radius} \leq \textrm{diameter} \leq 2 \cdot \textrm{radius}]
